claims.text: A lower-temperature secondary annealing step can induce nanoscale precipitates in a homogenized magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The secondary annealing can form nanoscale precipitates without changing the alloy's overall composition.
The processing can preserve the overall phase content while introducing nanoscale precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates act as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
The precipitates disrupt domain alignment under an external magnetic field.
Hindered domain-wall motion makes magnetization reversal more difficult and thereby increases coercivity.
A two-step heat-treated sample will have a higher coercive field than a composition-matched sample subjected only to standard homogenization.
The predicted coercivity increase will appear as an increase in magnetic hysteresis-loop width.
The proposed effect is expected to hold for bulk samples measured at room temperature under matched magnetic-field orientations.
Variations in precipitate size or volume fraction, and uncontrolled precipitate coarsening, may limit the coercivity increase.
Precipitates larger than an optimal size range for domain-wall pinning may fail to increase coercivity.
The baseline is a homogenized alloy with a low density of precipitates.

contradictions.description: The conditions require preservation of overall phase content while the structural mediator requires formation of new precipitates. Unless 'overall phase content' is intended to exclude a minor nanoscale precipitate phase, these statements are in tension.
